stemBlocks.value: The graph shows two straight lines L and M, crossing at the marked point P. (a) Write down the coordinates of P. (b) State the solution of y = 2x − 1 and y = −x + 5. (c) Determine the equation of each line from the graph.
Think first: Read the crossing point and the two y-intercepts straight from the grid, then get each gradient by counting squares.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p133-q02 from workbook page 133.

solutionSteps.instruction: Read the coordinates of the marked intersection.

contentBlocks.value: P sits 2 across and 3 up from the origin

solutionSteps.instruction: State the solution of the simultaneous pair.

contentBlocks.value: The lines y = 2x − 1 and y = −x + 5 are L and M, and they meet only at P
L cuts the y-axis at -1 and rises 2 for every 1 across, so m = 2 and c = -1
M cuts the y-axis at 5 and falls 1 for every 1 across, so m = -1 and c = 5

solutionSteps.instruction: Check by substituting P into both equations.

strategyBlocks.value: Read P off the grid, use it as the simultaneous solution, then for each line read the y-intercept and count the rise over the run to get the gradient.

whyThisWorks.value: In the form y = mx + c the number c is the height at which the line crosses the y-axis and m is the amount y changes for a one-unit increase in x. Both can be read directly from a grid, which is why a graph carries the whole equation. The crossing point is the one pair of values that lies on both lines, so it is the solution of the two equations taken together.

commonErrors.misconception: Giving the gradient of M as 1 instead of -1 by ignoring that the line falls as x increases.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Giving the gradient of M as 1 instead of -1 by ignoring that the line falls as x increases.

commonErrors.misconception: Reading the y-intercept where the line crosses the x-axis.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Reading the y-intercept where the line crosses the x-axis.
Avoid this: Writing the intersection as (3, 2).

examTip.value: Count the gradient over a whole number of squares — go across 1 and read the rise, or across 2 and halve — so you never guess a slope.
